job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Chloe Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for anything. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my parents in a terraced house in Wrexham, in the small back bedroom. I get up at seven, help my mother with breakfast before she goes to her job as a school cook, and then I sit at the dining table with the laptop and the job listings. Most weeks I write out my applications by hand first, because it helps me think, and then type them up. On Thursdays I sing in the choir at our church, which is the one thing in the week I don't skip.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you study, and what was your final project?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Electrical engineering, with a focus on power. I passed, though not well, because I'm slow at exams and I don't like rushing. My final project was a monitoring unit for the wiring in our village hall, which tells the caretaker when a circuit is overloaded, and the committee still uses it. I did no internship, because the local firms said they only take students who already have a family contact.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, I'm glad it's not a revolution, because the world needs stable ground. At church and at home I'd say honest work is honest work, and a computer can't take that away. I'd say very little online. I don't think the internet is the place for opinions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, nothing changes for me, and that's the trouble. I need a job, and there are very few in power engineering near here. The ones at the grid company want experience, and the ones at local electricians want a van licence and three years on site. I keep thinking if I'd done an apprenticeship instead of a degree I'd be earning by now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, about five a week, and I'd ask my father's old friend, who runs a small electrical firm, whether I could shadow his team for a few days. I'd write to the college about a short course in electrical testing, which would give me a paper that firms recognise. And I'd carry on with the choir and the church work, because it keeps me steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worn down, mostly. I'm grateful for a quiet world, but it doesn't help with rent money for my parents' sake, and I feel I'm a burden on them. My mother never says it, but I can see her counting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd have done better with an apprenticeship. What makes you say that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Gareth did one at sixteen and earns more than me, with no debt, and has a van. I wouldn't change my degree, I'm proud of it, but I'd tell younger people to look at both a degree and an apprenticeship. Nobody told me the degree might be a harder road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel to be a burden, as you put it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I contribute when I can, around eighty pounds from the odd cleaning job at the church hall. But my father is on a night shift at the depot and my mother works six hours a day for little. I'd like to hand over a proper wage, and I can't, which is the part that eats at me.

say: I'd say I'm glad it's not a revolution, because the world needs **stable ground**.
At church I'd say honest work can't be taken away by a computer.
think: Nothing changes, and that is the trouble: very few **power engineering** jobs nearby.
Maybe an apprenticeship would have had me earning by now.
do: Apply to about five jobs a week and ask my father's friend to let me **shadow** his firm.
Write to the college about a short **electrical testing** course.
Keep up the choir and church hall work.
feel: **Worn down**, though grateful for a quiet world.
I feel like a **burden** on my parents.
S0.quote: I'd tell younger people to look at both a degree and an apprenticeship. Nobody told me the degree might be a harder road.

Enrol in a short electrical testing course at the college

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have to be careful, and keep people at the centre of work. At church I'd say a machine can write a letter but can't sit with someone who is grieving. I'd say very little online, but I'd sign a petition that asked for jobs to be kept for local people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the office parts of my work, the drawings, the calculations and the reports, are the parts that go. The parts that stay are the ones with a ladder and a screwdriver. I'm trained for the first kind and I'd have to learn the second, which I'm willing to do but I'm slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push harder for a hands-on start, the electrician's route, even if it means working as a mate for a few years. I'd ask the college about an apprenticeship that takes graduates. I still wouldn't use the AI tools. I don't trust them, and I'd rather make my own mistakes than someone else's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but at least I can see a place to put my hands. I feel more settled than I did with the first picture, which is odd.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't use the tools. What would that cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a few jobs, I know. When firms ask if you've used these systems, they'd mark me down. But I'd rather lose a job than lose the habit of thinking for myself, and I think there'll be firms who agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that things are changing, but good work will always be needed. My father would say learn a trade, he's said it for years. I'd tell him he was right all along, and he'd smile, which I'd like to see.

fieldNote: She **accepts** that her stance may cost her jobs and holds to it.
Moves toward a trade route, in line with her traditional outlook.
Her father's advice about trades comes back as vindication.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it is far too fast, and that our leaders should have prepared people years ago. At church I'd ask us to pray and to look after each other. I wouldn't say much online, but I'd write to our councillor and member of parliament, in ink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it feels like a flood. The thinking work I studied for goes in two years. Robots for hands-on work come in 2031, and I don't know if I'd be good enough by then. I can't see how I'd afford to retrain, with debt and eighty pounds a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the church and ask whether anyone knew of any work, because people help each other here. I'd take any job with my hands, cleaning, care, warehouse, to bring money in. And I'd talk to my parents about whether we should all stay in the house together and share costs, which we already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and a little ashamed to be so. I trust in God and in my family, but I'd lie awake. I'd feel the whole thing is moving faster than a person can think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that I won't leave them, and that I'll work at whatever I can find. My mother would say we've been through harder times, and she'd mention the mines closing when she was a girl. I'd try to believe her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a short warning change, compared with a longer one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With a short warning I can't hope for a slow route like an apprenticeship. I'd have to take what's there. With a longer one, I could go the proper way and learn a trade over four years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to prepare if we don't waste it. At church I'd tell the young ones to learn a trade and keep faith. I'd write to the council about apprenticeships and I'd support any party that backs them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years is the proper length for what I want to do: a real apprenticeship or a recognised qualification, then a few years' work. By 2031 I'd be qualified and earning. By 2034, when robots come to hands-on work, I'd have savings and some choices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to an electrical apprenticeship and a college course at the same time. I'd keep the cleaning job and stay with my parents to save money. After a year of that, I'd have enough to put down a small amount on something, maybe, or help my parents with their bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the two-year one. It's a picture I can walk into. I'd be nervous at the start, but I'd feel I was doing honest things in the right order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does the order matter so much to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen people rush and ruin themselves. My uncle sold his house for a business and lost it in a year. I'd rather do the slow, proper thing, with a qualification and no debts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the apprenticeship places are all taken?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd do the college course in the evenings and work for any electrician who'd have me. I'd ask at church, since half the congregation knows a tradesman. It's a worse path, but still a path.

I'd tell young people at church to learn a trade and keep faith.

By 2034 I'd have savings and some choices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and we must teach the young properly. At church I'd say patience will pay. I'd write to my councillor to ask for more apprenticeships in the area, because it's the kind of thing a local body can actually do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, ten years lets me do the whole path: qualify, work, save and maybe have a family. I'd be thirty-three in 2036 and could be a proper electrician with my own tools. I'd like to think the robots in 2039 would still need someone to oversee them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd find any work in the first year and sign up for the apprenticeship, then the qualification. I'd save a bit every month, and when I was twenty-seven I'd think about a house. I'd also look after my parents as they get older. They'd count on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quiet and hopeful, but I'd not get carried away. The worry is that ten years goes by and I've drifted. I need to be careful not to be slow to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned family. What would you want by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A husband I'd met through church or work, maybe two children, and a house with a garden. I'd want my parents nearby, in their own place. I think a lot of this comes down to having something steady to come home to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help you not drift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A mentor, to be honest. Someone who checks in every few months, like a tradesman from church. I'd also write my goals down in a notebook each January, and read them again in December.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. There'd be no time to do things in the proper order, and I'd be left grabbing at any job. What would help is real apprenticeships near here for people like me, and employers who'd take a chance on a graduate who isn't flashy.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people assume a graduate has choices. I have a degree and a debt and a room in my parents' house, and not much else. I'd say to anyone in my position: don't be ashamed, and look after your people.

headlineQuote: I have a degree and a debt and a room in my parents' house, and not much else.
portrait: **Chloe**, 23, passed electrical engineering and lives in her parents' small back bedroom in Wrexham, with a church choir she won't skip.
Her father works nights at a depot and her mother is a school cook, so there is **no spare money**.
Traditional and resistant, she distrusts AI tools, likes doing things in the **proper order** and values family and faith.
She leans toward apprenticeships and trade work, which she thinks she should have started with.
Her mood is anxious in slower worlds and alarmed when the warning is short, because the slow route disappears.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world worries her most: no time to do things in order and a risk of rushing.
She fears being a burden on her parents.
whatWouldHelp: Employers who take a chance on a graduate who isn't flashy.
